Let us now perform a Ljung-Box test for the null hypothesis that the residuals after fitting the ARIMA model are white noise. s = 4 # choose based on frequency of data # e.g. monthly data s=12, quarterly s=4, weekly s=4 or 5 seasonality = TRUE # parameter if (seasonality) {lag1 = 2*s} else {lag1 = 10} T1 = length(petrolchanged$Cost); threshold = T1/5 if (lag1>threshold) {lag1 = round(threshold)} arimafit = petrol %>% model(mod = ARIMA(box_cox(Cost,lvalue))) dof1 = arimafit %>% coef() %>% dim() %>% first() augment(arimafit) %>% features(.innov, ljung_box, lag=lag1, dof=dof1) ## # A tibble: 1 × 3 ## .model lb_stat lb_pvalue ## <chr> <dbl> <dbl> ## 1 mod 14.6 0.0240 According to Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2021), it is advisable to choose our lag to be \(\min(10, n/5 \approx 140) = 10\) for this test, where \(n\) is the number of observations in our time series. Hence, we choose our lag to be 10 and we have 5 degrees of freedom (for two AR parameters and 3 MA parameters). The resulting p-value is 0.542, well above any typical significance level such as 0.05. Insurance companies are not allowed to discriminate based on race or age of housing, called ‘redlining’. Our primary interest is to study whether they did discriminate based on these factors in Chicago after taking other factors into account. If the extent of redlining is significant, the state could pursue a case to reprimand the behaviour of the Chicago insurance industry, or they could investigate particular insurance companies more deeply. 3.2 Setting up the data Our data is identified according to zip codes and we have variables for race (in % minority), fire (per 1,000 housing units), theft (per 1,000 housing units), age (% of units built in or before 1939), income (median family income in 10,000 US dollars), voluntary market activity (per 100 housing units) and involuntary market activity (per 100 housing units). Note that income has been divided by 10,000 so that regression coefficients are easier to write down. There are 47 zip codes in the dataset. 3.2.1 The observations Figure 1 – Dendrogram created using hierarchical clustering of covariates between zip codes We compare the dendrogram to a map of Chicago and merge the adjacent zip codes as in Figure 2. Figure 2 – Map of Chicago in 1977/78 with ‘similar’ zip codes coloured The data we have is classified according to zip codes and we may have an issue regarding independence between observations (an assumption for standard linear models). Our proposed solution to this is to merge some of zip codes together. We use hierarchical clustering to determine which zip codes exhibit the most similar characteristics with regards to the scaled covariates (race, fire, theft, age and income). We exclude the response from this process as we want to provide a possible legal case for redlining and do not want to fit a model that will be biased towards the result that we want. Above a certain point in the Euclidean-distance dendrogram created by hierarchical clustering, as shown in Figure 1, we merge any zip codes that are adjacent to each other on a map of Chicago at the time. The choice of cut-off was motivated by comparing dendrograms created using ‘complete’ linkage versus ‘single’ linkage and seeing which of the same groups were formed. (Intuitively speaking, complete linkage looks at the farthest Euclidean distance between covariates in groups, while single linkage looks at the closest.) Another motivation for the cut-off is to retain a sufficient number of observations in our dataset. There is a question on how exactly we should merge the data between the zip codes. We decide to simply take the mean of all variables data collected for the zip codes in the same group and regard it as a single zip code observation. This is arguably reasonable as the postcodes are supposed to have similar values for the covariates, and fire and theft are already standardised to every 1,000 housing units. The number of zip codes is reduced from 47 to 33. 3.2.2 The variables The variables voluntary market activity and involuntary market activity are effectively the number of accepted insurance policies and rejected insurance policies respectively. Since we will use a standard linear model, we can only have one response variable, so we define a new variable, \[ AcceptRate = \left( \frac{\text{Voluntary market activity}} {\text{Voluntary market activity} + (\text{Involuntary market activity} + 0.01)} \right), \] and \[ Accept = \Phi^{-1}(AcceptRate), \] where \(\Phi^{-1}\) is the inverse of the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution (i.e. the probit function). Our final response variable will be Accept, but AcceptRate is a useful intermediate result. AcceptRate is a proportion variable between 0 and 1 non-inclusive. Applying the probit function allows us to match the range of the response with the range of linear predictor of the regression, while also making the response look more bell-shaped. 3.3 Standard Linear Model We proceed to fit a linear model to the data using the standard lm function in R. Our strategy will be to fit the best possible model with Accept as the response and fire, theft and income as the covariates. Then, we will use added variable plots to check if race or age is relevant to the regression. 3.3.1 Exploratory Data Analysis pairs(cbind(AcceptRate,covar),main="Pairs Plot of Insurance Data",panel=function(x,y){points(x,y);lines(lowess(x,y))}) Figure 3 - Pairs plot of insurance data Prior to fitting our model, we will make a few plots using our initial covariates. We will use AcceptRate rather than Accept in these plots as they are roughly distributed in the same way, but AcceptRate is always between 0 and 1, which will be more interpretable on the vertical axis. The pairs plot of our initial covariates and AcceptRate is shown in Figure 3. As expected, we see some clear correlations between AcceptRate and Fire, and AcceptRate and Income, which are negative and positive respectively. Theft alone appears to be a poor determinant of AcceptRate. There also does not appear to be a multicollinearity problem between the covariates. However, our purpose here is slightly different. We want to lean slightly more towards explaining Accept as much as possible using only fire, theft and income. Then if we can show that race or age is still relevant, the argument that redlining is occurring may be more convincing to a legal authority. We employ exhaustive variable selection including all squared and interaction terms. Some results are shown in Figure 6. We can see that the best model according to Mallow’s \(C_p\) criterion should have three variables, while according to adjusted \(R^{2}\), the best model should have five variables (leading to an adjusted \(R^{2}\) of 92.8%). The plots in Figure 9 show that both race or age are not relevant in a model that accounts for fire, fire2, income and the interaction term between fire and income. There is no strong apparent pattern in either plot. The plot for race might a slight linear relationship, but the correlation is low (about 30% in magnitude). Additionally, a straight-line fit either directly in the plot or in a regression with the four chosen variables plus race does not output a significant p-value at the 5% significance level (the p-values are 0.084 and 0.107 respectively). It should be noted that these plots were created using the lm function in R. If, however, we fit the added variable plot for race using robust linear regression (rlm), the straight-line fit actually does become significant at the 5% level. However, it quickly returns to being insignificant once we remove the high-leverage observation 3 from our dataset, implying that the relationship is not important. 3.5 Conclusion The final model we have chosen is Equation 1 in section 3.3. Our purpose in this report was to study whether race or age were relevant in accepted or rejected insurance policies in order to determine whether redlining was occurring in Chicago between December 1977 and February 1978. Initial symbol co-plots indicated that race or age may be relevant. Once we fit the best model we could using fire, theft and income, we investigated whether race or age was still relevant. The added variable plots showed that they were not and there is no substantive evidence of redlining.

Chapter 4 Introduction Treatment of chickenpox (varicella) cases uses up significant economic resources in Hungary. The Hungarian authorities were interested in the past in determining whether widespread distribution of a chickenpox vaccine would be appropriate (Meszner, Molnar, Rampakakis, Yang, Kuter, & Lara, 2017). The data used for this project are 521 weekly Hungarian chickenpox case counts by county from 2005 to 2014 inclusive, with Budapest regarded as its own administrative region. This data were provided publicly by Rozemberczki, Scherer, Kiss, Sarkar, and Ferenci (2021) and downloaded from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (University of California, 2021). The decision to make vaccines publicly available was already approved in 2018 (“Hungary to provide chickenpox vaccine”, 2018). Nevertheless, the data set may still be able to provide additional insights. My research question is to study whether population density plays a role in the behaviour of the time series. I am interested in whether higher population density may result in a greater number of “super-spreader” events. One key factor will be seasonality in the data set, as it is thought that that colder seasons and the timing of the school year have a significant effect on chickenpox cases (Rozemberczki et al., 2021). This may have different effects in the regions of differing population density. A natural choice in answering this research question is to fit multiplicative seasonal ARIMA models to the chickenpox case numbers, as we can study both seasonality and the case-number dependence on previous values and forecast errors. We will do so for four chosen Hungarian regions.

Chapter 6 Methodology 6.1 Initial setup This project will use R to fit Bayesian models (R Core Team, 2021). The interface used to write in R is RStudio (RStudio Team, 2021). The Stan programming language is indirectly used (Carpenter et al., 2017). Please see Appendices ?? and ?? for R packages used and R code respectively. The aggregation into monthly data was done computationally using the fpp3 package in R, which automatically loads some packages in the tidyverse collection of packages (Hyndman, 2021). This reduces the number of observations to 120 months’ worth of case counts, of which we will take 108 as training data and 12 as test data. Finally, as discussed in Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2021), fpp3 is used to determine the value for \(\lambda\) in a Box-Cox transformation, in order to adjust for heteroskedasticity in the time series. Assuming the untransformed monthly series is \((x_t)\), this transformation is achieved for non-zero \(\lambda\) via the formula \(y_t = (x_t^\lambda - 1)/\lambda\). Central to our methodology is the R package bayesforecast, which interfaces with the programming language Stan, to fit Bayesian time series models (Alonzo & Cruz, 2020). 6.2 Order selection bayesforecast used for ARIMA order selection, the algorithm for which is described below. Note that the process compares the BIC of frequentist fittings to find the preferred order. Firstly, the following constraints are made for a multiplicative seasonal ARIMA model \[ y_t \sim SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_{12} \] \(p + q + P + Q \leq 6\) \(d + D \leq 2\) \(0 \leq p \leq 5, 0 \leq d \leq 2, 0 \leq q \leq 5\) \(0 \leq P \leq 2, 0 \leq D \leq 2, 0 \leq Q \leq 2\) Steps for model selection, with exhaustive search and approximations off (stepwise=FALSE, approximation=FALSE), are based on the algorithm by Hyndman and Khandakar (2008). The first two steps are used to ensure stationarity. Use Kwiatkowski–Phillips–Schmidt–Shin test(s) to determine \(d\). Use the period of an STL decomposition to determine \(D\). Exhaustively check the BIC of all possible models within the constraints to determine the preferred \(\{p,d,q,P,D,Q\}\). 6.3 Prior and posterior distributions 6.3.1 Sampling model As previously, take \((x_t)\) as the untransformed monthly series. Note that the numbers of parameters \(p\) varies depending on our four time series, but the maximum number of parameters fitted in one model is 6 and the minimum is 5. The initial parameter values are randomly generated (Stan Development Team, 2021). The following algorithm is repeated 4 times, so that we have 4 chains. Algorithm steps Repeat the following steps for each iteration from \(i = 1,\ldots,2000\). The burn-in period will be half of the iterations. Thinning is not required. Recall that, at its maximum number of parameters, \(\mathbf{\gamma} = \left( \mu,\sigma,\phi,\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2},\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\Theta_{1},\Theta_{2} \right)\). Let the superscript in brackets correspond to the iteration number. Hence define the joint distribution of all parameters \[ \begin{aligned} p\left( \mathbf{\gamma}|\mathbf{\gamma}^{(i - 1)} \right) ={}& p\left( \mu \middle| \mathbf{y},\mathbf{\epsilon},\mathbf{\gamma}_{- \mu}^{(i - 1)} \right)\ p\left( \sigma \middle| \mathbf{y},\mathbf{\epsilon},\mathbf{\gamma}_{- \sigma}^{(i - 1)} \right)\ p\left( \phi \middle| \mathbf{y},\mathbf{\epsilon},\mathbf{\gamma}_{- \phi}^{(i - 1)} \right) \\ &\times p\left( \Phi_{1} \middle| \mathbf{y},\mathbf{\epsilon},\mathbf{\gamma}_{- \Phi_{j}}^{(i - 1)} \right)\ p\left( \Phi_{2} \middle| \mathbf{y},\mathbf{\epsilon},\mathbf{\gamma}_{- \Phi_{j}}^{(i - 1)} \right)\ p\left( \theta_{1} \middle| \mathbf{y},\mathbf{\epsilon},\mathbf{\gamma}_{- \theta_{k}}^{(i - 1)} \right) \\ &\times p\left( \theta_{2} \middle| \mathbf{y},\mathbf{\epsilon},\mathbf{\gamma}_{- \theta_{k}}^{(i - 1)} \right)\ p\left( \Theta_{1} \middle| \mathbf{y},\mathbf{\epsilon},\mathbf{\gamma}_{- \Theta_{l}}^{(i - 1)} \right)\ p\left( \Theta_{2} \middle| \mathbf{y},\mathbf{\epsilon},\mathbf{\gamma}_{- \Theta_{l}}^{(i - 1)} \right) \\ &\times \left\{ \prod_{i = 37}^{108}{p\left( \epsilon_{t} \middle| \mathbf{y},\mathbf{\epsilon}_{- \left\{ \geq t \right\}},\mathbf{\gamma}^{(i - 1)} \right)} \right\} \end{aligned} \] At iteration \(i\) of the sampling algorithm: Step 1 If \(i \leq 1000\), set \(M = I_{p}\). Otherwise, set \(M\) as the reciprocal of the diagonal values from the covariance matrix of \(\mathbf{\gamma}^{(i = 1000)}\). Step 2 Draw \(\rho\ \sim\ N_{p}(0,M)\) and \(\epsilon_{t}\ \sim\ N(0,sd = \sigma)\). Step 3: Generate proposal values Let \(\mathbf{\gamma}^{\mathbf{*}} = \mathbf{\gamma}^{(i - 1)}\). Solve the differential equations \[\frac{d\mathbf{\gamma}^{\mathbf{*}}}{dt} = - \frac{d\log\left( p(\rho) \right)}{d\rho},\ \ \frac{d\rho}{dt} = \frac{d\log{p\left( \mathbf{\gamma}^{\mathbf{*}}|\mathbf{\gamma}^{(i - 1)} \right)}}{d\mathbf{\gamma}^{\mathbf{*}}},\] to obtain \(\mathbf{\gamma}^{\mathbf{*}}\). The way to solve these differential equations is complex and beyond the scope of this project. The no-U-Turn sampler uses a unique ‘leapfrog’ algorithm that involves binary trees (Stan Development Team, 2021). Step 4: Metropolis-like step Let \(H\left( \rho,\mathbf{\gamma} \right) = - \log{p(\rho) - \log{p\left( \mathbf{\gamma} \right)}}\) Step 4a: Compute acceptance ratio \[r = \exp\left\{ H\left( \rho,\mathbf{\gamma}^{(i - 1)} \right) - H\left( \rho,\mathbf{\gamma}^{*} \right) \right\}\] Step 4b: Set \(\mathbf{\gamma}^{(i)} = \mathbf{\gamma}^{*}\) if \(r > 1\) and to \(\mathbf{\gamma}^{(i - 1)}\) otherwise. Step 5: Predict the value of \(y_{t}\), called \(\widehat{y_{t}}\) (see Equation (6.2)), using the parameter values in \(\mathbf{\gamma}^{(i)}\), Step 6: Set \(\epsilon_{t}^{(i)} = y_{t} - \widehat{y_{t}}\). 6.5 Posterior predictive checks After the algorithm is complete, extract all the columns of \(\mathbf{\gamma} = \left( \mu,\sigma,\phi,\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2},\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\Theta_{1},\Theta_{2} \right)\) as MCMC chains. For our posterior predictive checks, we will use the Arima function from the forecast package to simulate seasonal ARIMA models with fixed coefficient values. Our main test statistic will be to compare the model, which used 108 observations, to compare to the full set of 120 observations by simulating 120 observations. Two other test statistics will be used – the ACF and PACF of the 120 observations, as these describe the dependence structure of the time series. These posterior checks will be conducted against the original data set, aggregated to monthly data, i.e. prior to the Box-Cox transformation, and with the estimated mean parameter subtracted. The algorithm for posterior predictive draws will work as follows. For 1,000 loops: From the post burn-in set of \(\mathbf{\gamma}\) values, draw a particular row from the coefficient matrix (i.e. parameters from the same iteration). Use the Arima function to simulate the appropriate ARIMA model with coefficients fixed to those that were drawn in step 1. Calculate the test statistics for these simulations. Calculate the proportion of times whether the test statistics exceed the statistics from the real data set. Chapter 8 Discussion In our research question, we are interested in studying how population density may lead to differences in the behaviour of chickenpox case numbers over time. Part of this process is to fit the best ARIMA models we can. To interpret the meaning of the coefficients, the mean values of the coefficients are summarised in Table 8.1, with a blank entry indicating that the model order did not include that parameter. Recall that phi terms correspond to AR and seasonal AR coefficients, while theta terms correspond to respective MA coefficients. Table 8.1: ARIMA coefficients for each series Model \(\mu\) \(\sigma\) \(\phi\) \(\theta_{1}\) \(\theta_{2}\) \(\Phi_{1}\) \(\Phi_{2}\) \(\Theta_{1}\) \(\Theta_{2}\) Budapest 1.7 149.1 0.5 -0.4 -0.4 Pest -2.5 127.5 0.6 -0.7 Heves -2 84.2 0.7 -0.8 0.1 Somogy -4.6 59.4 0.5 0.2 -0.4 It should be noted that all of the 90% credible intervals for \(\mu\) included 0 and the size of \(\mu\) is not large compared to the scale of actual cases which are often in the hundreds. The values of \(\sigma\) are not of concern as it is not the focus of our research question. All of the ARIMA coefficients had fairly narrow 90% credible intervals, where the width of the intervals was at most about 0.4 and could be as small as 0.2. The only credible interval that included 0 was \(\Theta_{2}\) for the Heves series. Seasonality is certainly present in the time series and cases or forecast errors up to 24 months prior (in the same month of the year) can affect the current timestep. We can interpret that the Budapest series has the strongest dependence on previous values of its series, both immediately prior and in the same month in previous years. All the series showed a dependence on the case numbers from the month prior, except for Somogy. The Budapest series was the only one that did not use past forecast errors, while Somogy was the only series that used past forecast errors from the months immediately prior. Overall, we can see that these four regions that have the largest differences in population density behave quite differently, which suggests our research question has merit. Although the sample size in terms of the number of time series studied is small, we possibly see a sort of shift from AR and seasonal AR terms being important in regions of high population density to MA and seasonal MA terms playing a larger role in smaller population density regions. Seasonality clearly plays a factor here, as the shift from AR to MA terms occurs in both the seasonal and non-seasonal components.

Chapter 9 Conclusion My research question involved looking into the way population density affects the behaviour of chickenpox cases in Hungary. Four time series were chosen that were the farthest apart from each other in terms of population density. Although we only studied a small number of time series, we did see that there was a clear difference in the order of ARIMA fitted moving from the highest population density series to the lowest population density series. This difference can be described as a shift from seasonal and non-seasonal AR coefficients to seasonal and non-seasonal MA coefficients. In other words, in our small sample, for higher population density regions, chickenpox cases were more dependent on chickenpox cases in previous periods or the same month in previous years, while the numbers for lower population regions were more dependent on seasonal and non-seasonal forecast errors. Seasonality, particularly the timing of school holidays, played a significant role in determining this effect. One of the strengths of our analysis is that the ARIMA model fitting was Bayesian. Although we did not have a small data set, adapting the method used in this project for a much shorter time series would not be difficult and the results would likely be robust due to the structure provided by the prior distributions. There are some limitations in this analysis. There appeared to be an issue in simulating some (but not all) series with MA parameters. This was easily fixed by repeatedly simulating until there are no NA values, but may indicate some other issues with my code. If I had more time, I would program my own ARIMA evaluation function rather than using the forecast package. There are several extensions that could be suggested for this analysis. Though once the order was determined, we used a Bayesian method to fit the ARIMA model, the actual process for order selection was frequentist. In other words, the process exhaustively fitted models using frequentist estimation and compared the BIC of these values. It would be easy in principle to replace the frequentist estimation with Bayesian estimation, but this would be very time-consuming to run. Other model selection criteria could be used too, such as leave-one-out cross-validation. There appeared to be a slight misfit for the Pest series in terms of forecast accuracy and residual checks. However, the ARIMA order was determined exhaustively using a frequentist method. It may be beneficial to investigate alternative orders to see if the Bayesian fitting could be improved. Finally, another obvious extension is to study more than one series simultaneously using a vector autoregressive method or a hierarchical method.
